subject: Sample: an AOG parts desk, and what it would have to earn
preheader: Sample issue for the aviation section. The products and the sponsor below are fictional.

lead.title: An AOG desk only pays if the aircraft gets back in service sooner
lead.summary: This sample lead is about how an airline or MRO would judge an AI tool for aircraft-on-ground recovery. The product named later in the issue, AOGLine, is not real. The point of the sample is the shape of the briefing: one lead, a few tools, a playbook, a short link list, and labeled sponsor slots.
lead.whyItMatters: An operation makes money on this category only when the tool shortens the time an aircraft sits, or when it avoids a premium parts buy that a planner would have made under pressure. If a controller still has to rebuild the plan by hand, the subscription is a cost, not a gain.

tools.name: AOGLine
tools.summary: Fictional sample. A recovery desk that ranks parts, loaners, and ferry options when an aircraft is on the ground.
tools.whyItMatters: Used on last month's AOG events, it can show whether a recovery plan gets shorter before anyone risks a live work order.
tools.pricing: Sample pricing, not a live offer.

tools.name: Baywright
tools.summary: Fictional sample. Turns a maintenance visit into a bay plan, with the cards, parts, and people the visit actually needs.
tools.whyItMatters: A fuller bay means fewer hours sold at a discount because the package arrived incomplete.
tools.pricing: Sample pricing, not a live offer.

tools.name: Stockramp
tools.summary: Fictional sample. Flags a premium parts buy before it is placed, and points at stock already on the shelf.
tools.whyItMatters: One avoided premium buy can cover a tool subscription. The gain is the buy you do not make.
tools.pricing: Sample pricing, not a live offer.

playbook.title: How an MRO would trial an AOG tool
playbook.intro: This playbook is sample guidance for the format. It is not advice for any airline, shop, or operator.
steps: Pick one station or one fleet, not the whole network.
Run the tool on last month's AOG events first.
Have a planner check every suggestion before it changes a work order.
Track aircraft downtime against the subscription for two weeks.
Keep the tool only if recovered time covers the cost twice over.
